stem: A capacitor discharges through a resistor. What fraction of its initial charge remains after one time constant?

options.rationale: Correct: Q = Q₀e⁻¹ at t = RC.
That is after the half-time, 0.693RC.
63% is the fraction lost (or the fraction reached when charging).
An exponential never reaches zero; after 5RC less than 1% remains.

explanation: At t = RC, Q = Q₀e⁻¹ ≈ 0.37Q₀.

stem: Which correctly shows that the product RC has the unit of time?

options.rationale: Correct: a coulomb per ampere is a second.
Ω = V A⁻¹ and F = C V⁻¹, not V A and C V.
These are the reciprocals of the ohm and the farad.
J C⁻¹ is the volt, not the ohm, and J V⁻¹ is a coulomb, not a second.

explanation: Ω = V/A and F = C/V, so Ω F = C/A = (A s)/A = s.

stem: What is the time constant of a $220\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor discharging through a $10\ \text{k}\Omega$ resistor?

options.rationale: This multiplies 10 × 220 without the powers of ten.
This is the half-time, 0.693RC.
Correct: RC = 10 × 10³ × 220 × 10⁻⁶.
This loses a factor of 1000 in the prefixes.

explanation: $\tau = RC = 10 \times 10^{3} \times 220 \times 10^{-6} = 2.2\ \text{s}$.

stem: During the discharge of a capacitor through a fixed resistor, which statement about the current is correct?

options.content: It stays constant until the capacitor is empty, then falls to zero.
options.rationale: The current falls as the p.d. falls; it is never constant.

options.content: It decreases linearly to zero in a time RC.
options.rationale: The decrease is exponential, not linear.

options.content: It decays exponentially with the same time constant as the p.d.
options.rationale: Correct: I = V/R, so I is proportional to V.

options.content: It increases as the capacitor discharges.
options.rationale: A smaller p.d. drives a smaller current through R.

explanation: I = V/R at every instant, and V decays exponentially, so I decays exponentially with the same τ = RC.

stem: A capacitor charged to $12\ \text{V}$ discharges through a resistor with $RC = 2.0\ \text{s}$. What is the p.d. after $3.0\ \text{s}$?

options.rationale: This uses e^(−RC/t), with the ratio inverted.
This is the charging formula: the p.d. rises, not falls.
This uses 10 as the base instead of e.
Correct: 12e^(−1.5).

stem: A graph of ln(V/V) against t is plotted for a discharging capacitor. Which describes it?

options.content: A straight line through the origin with gradient RC
options.rationale: The line does not pass through the origin, and the gradient is −1/RC.

options.content: A straight line with negative gradient −1/RC and intercept ln V₀
options.rationale: Correct: ln V = ln V₀ − t/RC.

options.content: A curve that approaches zero asymptotically
options.rationale: That is the V-t graph; taking logs makes it straight.

options.content: A straight line with negative gradient −RC and intercept V₀
options.rationale: The gradient is −1/RC and the intercept is ln V₀, not V₀.

explanation: Taking ln of V = V₀e^(−t/RC) gives ln V = ln V₀ − (1/RC)t: y = c + mx with m = −1/RC.
hints: Take natural logarithms of both sides.

stem: A capacitor discharges through resistor R. The experiment is repeated with the same capacitor, same initial p.d. and a resistor of 2R. Which statement is correct?

options.content: The initial current doubles and the time constant halves.
options.rationale: A larger resistance gives a smaller current and a slower discharge.

options.content: The initial current halves and the time constant is unchanged.
options.rationale: τ = RC depends on R.

options.content: The initial current is unchanged and the time constant doubles.
options.rationale: I₀ = V₀/R depends on R.

options.content: The initial current halves and the time constant doubles.
options.rationale: Correct: I₀ = V₀/R and τ = RC.

explanation: I₀ = V₀/(2R) is halved; τ = 2RC is doubled. The total charge that flows (the area under I-t) is unchanged, CV₀.
hints: Use I₀ = V₀/R and τ = RC.

stem: Calculate the time for the p.d. across a $1000\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor discharging through a $33\ \text{k}\Omega$ resistor to halve, in s, to three significant figures.
explanation: $t_{1/2} = RC\ln 2 = 33 \times 10^{3} \times 1000 \times 10^{-6} \times 0.693 = 22.9\ \text{s}$. $RC$ alone is the time to fall to 37%.
workedSolution: 1. $t_{1/2} = RC\ln 2 = 33 \times 10^{3} \times 1000 \times 10^{-6} \times 0.693 = 22.9\ \text{s}$. $RC$ alone is the time to fall to 37%.

stem: A $680\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor charged to $6.0\ \text{V}$ discharges through a $15\ \text{k}\Omega$ resistor. Calculate the time for the p.d. to fall to $1.5\ \text{V}$, in s, to three significant figures.
explanation:
1. $RC = 15 \times 10^{3} \times 680 \times 10^{-6} = 10.2\ \text{s}$.
2. $t = RC\ln\dfrac{V_0}{V} = 10.2 \times \ln 4.0 = 14.1\ \text{s}$ (two half-times).
3. Using lg instead of ln gives a value 2.30 times too small.
workedSolution:
1. 1. $RC = 15 \times 10^{3} \times 680 \times 10^{-6} = 10.2\ \text{s}$.
2. $t = RC\ln\dfrac{V_0}{V} = 10.2 \times \ln 4.0 = 14.1\ \text{s}$ (two half-times).
3. Using lg instead of ln gives a value 2.30 times too small.

stem: A $2200\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor charged to $10\ \text{V}$ discharges through a $4.7\ \text{k}\Omega$ resistor. Calculate the current after $5.0\ \text{s}$, in mA, to three significant figures.
A capacitor discharging through a $47\ \text{k}\Omega$ resistor takes $16.3\ \text{s}$ for its p.d. to halve. Calculate its capacitance, in µF, to three significant figures.
explanation: $t_{1/2} = 0.693RC$, so $C = \dfrac{16.3}{0.693 \times 47 \times 10^{3}} = 5.00 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{F} = 500\ \mu\text{F}$. Forgetting $\ln 2$ treats the half-time as the time constant.
workedSolution: 1. $t_{1/2} = 0.693RC$, so $C = \dfrac{16.3}{0.693 \times 47 \times 10^{3}} = 5.00 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{F} = 500\ \mu\text{F}$. Forgetting $\ln 2$ treats the half-time as the time constant.

stem: An uncharged $100\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor is charged through a $27\ \text{k}\Omega$ resistor from a $6.0\ \text{V}$ supply of negligible internal resistance. Calculate the p.d. across the capacitor after $4.0\ \text{s}$, in V, to three significant figures.
explanation: $RC = 2.7\ \text{s}$. $V = E(1 - e^{-t/RC}) = 6.0(1 - e^{-4.0/2.7}) = 4.64\ \text{V}$. The discharge formula would give the p.d. still to be gained, $1.36\ \text{V}$.
workedSolution: 1. $RC = 2.7\ \text{s}$. $V = E(1 - e^{-t/RC}) = 6.0(1 - e^{-4.0/2.7}) = 4.64\ \text{V}$. The discharge formula would give the p.d. still to be gained, $1.36\ \text{V}$.
hints: When charging, V rises towards E: V = E(1 − e^(−t/RC)).

stem: In each time interval equal to the half-time, a discharging capacitor loses the same fraction of its remaining charge.
explanation: True. Exponential decay removes a constant fraction (here one half) in each equal interval, not a constant amount.

stem: For a capacitor discharging through a resistor, match each graph feature with what it represents.

left.content: gradient of the charge-time graph at a point
gradient of the ln V against t graph
time for V to fall to 37% of V₀

right.content: minus the current at that instant
charge that has flowed off the capacitor

explanation: I = −dQ/dt; Q = ∫I dt; ln V = ln V₀ − t/RC; e⁻¹ ≈ 0.37.
hints: Current is the rate of flow of charge.

stem: Complete the explanation of the shape of the discharge curve.

payload.template: As charge flows off, the p.d. across the capacitor {{blank:a}}, so the current through the resistor {{blank:b}}, and charge is lost more {{blank:c}}. The rate of loss is proportional to the charge remaining.

explanation: dQ/dt = −Q/RC: smaller Q means a smaller rate of loss, so the curve flattens.

stem: What name is given to the product RC for a capacitor discharging through a resistor?
explanation: The **time constant** τ = RC, measured in seconds.

stem: Describe the graph of p.d. against time for a capacitor discharging through a resistor, as you would sketch it, marking two key points.

points.description: Starts at V₀ on the p.d. axis at t = 0.
Falls with the steepest gradient at t = 0; the gradient decreases continuously (curve concave upwards).
Marked points: 0.37V₀ at t = RC (and/or 0.5V₀ at 0.693RC).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The curve starts at V₀ at t = 0 and falls, steeply at first and then more and more gently, approaching the time axis without reaching it. At t = RC the p.d. is 0.37V₀, and at t = 0.693RC it is 0.5V₀.

explanation: Exponential decay curve.

stem: Explain why the discharge of a capacitor through a resistor is exponential.

points.description: The current is I = V/R = Q/(RC), proportional to the charge remaining.
The current is the rate of loss of charge: dQ/dt = −Q/RC.
A rate of decrease proportional to the quantity itself gives exponential decay, Q = Q₀e^(−t/RC).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: At any instant the current is I = V/R = Q/(RC), and this current is the rate at which charge leaves the capacitor, so dQ/dt = −Q/RC. A quantity whose rate of decrease is proportional to its own value decays exponentially: Q = Q₀e^(−t/RC).

explanation: Rate of loss ∝ amount remaining.
hints: Write the current in terms of Q.

stem: Describe how the current, the p.d. across the capacitor and the charge change while an uncharged capacitor is charged through a resistor from a d.c. supply.

points.description: Current starts at its maximum E/R and decays exponentially to zero (time constant RC).
The p.d. across the capacitor rises from zero towards E, quickly at first then levelling off.
The charge rises in the same way towards CE (63% after one time constant).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: At the instant of connection the capacitor has no p.d., so the current is E/R; as charge builds up the capacitor's p.d. opposes the supply, so the current decays exponentially with time constant RC. The p.d. and charge rise from zero towards E and CE along a curve that is steep at first and then levels off, reaching 63% after RC.

explanation: Charging: current decays; V and Q rise to their final values.
hints: What opposes the supply as the capacitor charges?

stem: A timer holds an irrigation valve open while the p.d. across a discharging $1000\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor is above $4.0\ \text{V}$. The capacitor is charged to $12\ \text{V}$ and then discharges through a resistor R. The valve must stay open for $60\ \text{s}$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the resistance R needed, in kΩ, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the energy stored in the capacitor at the start, in J, to two significant figures.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: State how the open time would change if R were doubled.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The time would double, because t = RC ln 3 is proportional to R.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Electrolytic capacitors have a tolerance of about ±20%. Explain the effect on the timer and suggest how the timer could be adjusted.

points.description: The actual time could differ by up to about 20% from 60 s (t ∝ C).
Use a variable resistor for R and calibrate the time with a stop-watch.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Since t is proportional to C, the open time could be up to about 20% longer or shorter than 60 s. Using a variable resistor for R lets the timer be calibrated against a stop-watch.

explanation: t = RC ln(V₀/V) for the time to fall from V₀ to V.
